name: Trader superday
models: Reported, as of Nov 2026: trading-firm final rounds at Jane Street, Optiver, SIG, IMC and Citadel Securities. Probability, mental maths, market-making games and fit questions.
description: This is the reported shape of a trading firm's final-round day, as candidates described it by Nov 2026. Jane Street, Optiver, SIG, IMC and Citadel Securities all report these rounds. They cover probability and betting games, mental maths, market-making games and fit questions. There are four papers, each on its own clock. Real rounds are spoken, so say each written answer aloud before you type it. Mental maths is one question at a time with no going back. No calculator is allowed. Orders and lengths differ by firm and office. Two checks at the end ask for what the app cannot see.

items.title: Four faces of six
items.question: A fair die is rolled until four different faces have appeared. What is the expected number of rolls?

options.why: You stopped once three faces had appeared. The fourth new face takes 2 rolls on average.
You waited 6 rolls for each face, as if you needed one particular face each time. Any new face will do.
You collected all six faces. Only four different faces are needed.

feedback.correct: Add the waits for each new face, $1 + \tfrac65 + \tfrac64 + \tfrac63$.
feedback.generic: Split the wait into stages: the first new face, then the second, and so on.

explain.text: With $k$ faces seen, a new face comes with chance $\tfrac{6-k}{6}$, so that stage takes $\tfrac{6}{6-k}$ rolls on average. The four stages add to $1 + 1.2 + 1.5 + 2 = 5.7$. A step-by-step solve on the number of faces seen gives the same.

items.title: Nobody gets their own hat
items.question: Four people leave their hats at a cloakroom. The hats are handed back in a random order. What is the chance that nobody gets their own hat?

options.why: You found the chance that somebody gets their own hat. The question asks for nobody.
You treated each person as missing their hat independently, $(\tfrac34)^4$. The hats are not independent.
You counted only the orders where the hats go round in one cycle, $3! = 6$ of 24. The 3 double swaps count too.

feedback.correct: 9 of the 24 orders give nobody their own hat.
feedback.generic: List the 24 orders, or use inclusion-exclusion on the people who get their own hat.

explain.text: By inclusion-exclusion the chance is $1 - 1 + \tfrac12 - \tfrac16 + \tfrac1{24} = \tfrac{9}{24} = \tfrac38$. Listing the 24 orders finds 9 with no fixed point: 6 four-cycles and 3 double swaps.

items.title: How much to stake
items.prose: You may stake any share of your bankroll on an even-money bet. You win it with chance 0.6. The bet repeats many times.
items.question: What share of your bankroll should you stake each time to maximise its long-run growth?

options.why: You maximised the expected value of one bet. One loss at 100% ends the game, so long-run growth is lost.
You staked the chance of winning. The stake depends on the edge, the win chance less the loss chance.
You read even money as odds of 2 to 1, from the £2 returned. Even money pays 1 to 1.

feedback.correct: For an even-money bet the stake is $p - q = 0.6 - 0.4$.
feedback.generic: Maximise the expected log of your bankroll after one bet.

explain.text: The log growth $0.6\ln(1+f) + 0.4\ln(1-f)$ peaks where $0.6(1-f) = 0.4(1+f)$, so $f = 0.2$. A grid in 1% steps also peaks at 20%, with growth of about 0.0201 a bet. Staking everything maximises the mean, but one loss ends the game.

items.title: A fair call from a biased coin
items.prose: A coin lands heads with chance 0.25. To make a fair call, you toss it in pairs. You stop at the first pair that is HT or TH.
items.question: What is the expected number of tosses?

options.why: You counted pairs, not tosses. Each pair is two tosses.
You waited for the first tail, $1/0.75$. The pair must hold one of each.
You waited for the first head, $1/0.25$. A head alone does not end the game.

feedback.correct: A pair ends it with chance $0.375$, so $\tfrac{2}{0.375}$ tosses.
feedback.generic: Find the chance that one pair ends the game.

explain.text: A pair is HT or TH with chance $2 \times 0.25 \times 0.75 = 0.375$. So the pairs average $\tfrac{1}{0.375}$, and the tosses $\tfrac{2}{0.375} = \tfrac{16}{3} \approx 5.33$. Solving $E = 2 + 0.625E$ gives the same.

items.title: When to bet on red
items.prompt:
Say your answer aloud first, then type it.

A deck of 26 red and 26 black cards is shuffled. The cards are turned over one at a time. At any moment you may stop and bet £1 that the next card is red. You win £1 if it is red and lose £1 if it is black. You must bet by the last card.

(a) What is the bet worth with your best play, and how should you play?

(b) The interviewer follows up. Now you may stake from £0 to £1 on either colour, on every card. What changes?
items.model:
**(a)** The question is whether any stopping rule beats betting at once. With $r$ red and $b$ black cards left, the next card is red with chance $\tfrac{r}{r+b}$. So stopping now is worth $\tfrac{r-b}{r+b}$ pounds. This is a fair game: one card later, its expected value is unchanged. So every stopping rule has expected gain £0. Check one red and one black card. Betting now gains 0. Waiting, the last card is red half the time, so 0 again. So the bet is worth £0, and how I play does not matter.

**(b)** With free stakes I can win. I stake £0 while the colours are level, and back the colour with more cards left otherwise. With one red and one black card, I stake £0 on the first, then £1 on the colour left. That gains £1 for sure.

rubric.text: States that the question is whether any stopping time helps
The next card is red with chance equal to the red share of the cards left
Gives the value of stopping now as the red-minus-black share, $\tfrac{r-b}{r+b}$
Argues that this is a fair game, so every stopping rule has expected gain 0
Checks a small deck by listing the cases
Answers £0 for the single bet
Says free stakes win, with the one-red, one-black example worth £1

items.title: Call or fold
items.prompt:
Say your answer aloud first, then type it.

You are heads-up and the pot holds £100. Your opponent bets £50. You think you win 30% of the time if you call.

(a) Do you call or fold? Show the numbers.

(b) The interviewer follows up. Say your hand beats only a bluff. How often must the £50 bet be a bluff for your call to break even?
items.model:
**(a)** Calling costs £50. If I win, I collect £150: the pot of £100 and their £50. So I need to win $\tfrac{50}{50 + 150} = 25\%$ of the time to break even. At 30% the call is worth $0.3 \times 150 - 0.7 \times 50 = +£10$. Check: $0.3 \times 200 - 50 = 10$. So I call. The 30% is my estimate, so I would test it against their range and how they have bet. A tighter player would push it down, and below 25% I fold.

**(b)** If a share $x$ of their bets are bluffs, calling gains $150x - 50(1 - x)$. That is 0 at $x = \tfrac14$. So the bet must be a bluff a quarter of the time, the same 25% as the pot odds.

rubric.text: States the price of the call, £50, and what it wins, £150
Break-even equity of 25% by a stated formula
EV of +£10 and the decision to call
Says the 30% is an estimate and what would change it
Bluff share of $\tfrac14$, with a reason
Reasons aloud in order and ends with a clear action

byKey.moved-point: You moved the decimal point one place too far. 13% of 760 is near 100, not 10.
byKey.ten-only: You took 10% only. Add the 3%, which is 22.8.

byKey.no-square: You squared 70 and stopped. Take off $2^2 = 4$.
byKey.squared: You squared 68. The second number is 72, not 68.

explain.text: 68 and 72 sit 2 either side of 70. So $68 \times 72 = 70^2 - 2^2 = 4900 - 4 = 4896$.

feedback.generic: Use $26 = 25 + 1$, or round 38 up to 40 and correct.

byKey.rounded: You rounded 38 up to 40 and did not correct. Take off $2 \times 26 = 52$.
byKey.digit: You slipped a digit in the tens. Check the last addition.

items.title: Two fractions as a decimal
items.question: Write $\tfrac18 + \tfrac1{12}$ as a decimal, to 3 places.

byKey.tops-bottoms: You added the tops and the bottoms, $\tfrac{2}{20}$. Use a common denominator, 24.
byKey.multiplied: You multiplied the fractions, $\tfrac{1}{96}$. The question asks for the sum.

explain.text: Over 24, $\tfrac18 = \tfrac{3}{24}$ and $\tfrac1{12} = \tfrac{2}{24}$, so the sum is $\tfrac{5}{24} \approx 0.208$. Check: $0.125 + 0.0833 = 0.2083$.

items.title: Eighteen years at 4%
items.question: Estimate $1.04^{18}$ to 2 decimal places. Answers within 0.03 count.

feedback.correct: By the rule of 72, 4% doubles in about 18 years.
feedback.generic: Use the rule of 72, or square four times.

byKey.simple: You added $18 \times 4\% = 72\%$. Growth compounds, so each year earns on the last.

explain.text: The rule of 72 says 4% doubles money in $72 / 4 = 18$ years, so the answer is near 2. Squaring gives $1.04^2 = 1.0816$, $1.04^4 \approx 1.1699$, $1.04^8 \approx 1.3686$ and $1.04^{16} \approx 1.8730$. Then $1.04^{18} = 1.04^{16} \times 1.04^2 \approx 2.026$.

feedback.generic: Pair the first number with the last.

byKey.stopped: You stopped at 119. The sum runs to 120, so add 120.
byKey.no-half: You worked out $120 \times 121$ and did not halve it.

explain.text: Pair 1 with 120, 2 with 119, and so on: 60 pairs, each adding to 121. So the sum is $60 \times 121 = 7260$, which is $\tfrac{120 \times 121}{2}$.

items.title: The last digit of a power
items.question: What is the last digit of $8^{2027}$?

feedback.generic: Write out the last digits of $8, 8^2, 8^3, 8^4$.

byKey.one-on: You went one step too far round the cycle. $2027 \bmod 4 = 3$, so take the third entry.
byKey.one-mod: You took $2027 \bmod 4$ as 2. It is 3, since 2024 is a multiple of 4.

explain.text: The last digits of the powers of 8 cycle 8, 4, 2, 6, every 4 steps. Since $2027 = 4 \times 506 + 3$, the last digit is the third in the cycle, 2.

items.title: Up, then down
items.question: A price rises 40%, then falls 25%. What is the net change, in percent? Write a fall as a negative number.

feedback.generic: Start at 100 and apply each change in turn.

byKey.added: You added the changes, $40 - 25$. The 25% fall is taken from the higher price.
byKey.multiplied: You took 40% of 25%. Apply the two changes one after the other.

explain.text: From 100, a 40% rise gives 140. A 25% fall takes off 35, leaving 105. So the net change is +5%, as $1.4 \times 0.75 = 1.05$.

items.title: A stack of coins
items.question: A coin is 2.5 mm thick. How tall, in km, is a stack of 1,000,000 coins? Choose the tightest interval that holds your estimate.

options.why: This sits wholly below the value, 2.5 km. Losing one zero between millimetres and metres lands here.
This sits wholly above the value, 2.5 km. You may have read 2.5 mm as 3.5 mm.
This holds the value, but 2.0 to 3.0 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.

feedback.correct: 2.0 to 3.0 holds the value, 2.5 km, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Multiply the figures step by step, rounding only at the end. Then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: A million coins of 2.5 mm make 2,500,000 mm, which is 2,500 m or 2.5 km. Check: 1,000 coins stand 2.5 m, and 1,000 such stacks stand 2.5 km. The interval 1.0 to 4.0 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less on the day.

items.title: Balls in a room
items.question: A room is 4 m by 5 m by 2.5 m. Balls 6.5 cm across fill 64% of its volume. How many balls are there, in thousands? Choose the tightest interval that holds your estimate.

options.why: This sits wholly above the value, about 222,500. Rounding the ball down to 6 cm lands near 283,000.
This holds the value, but 200 to 250 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.
This sits wholly below the value, about 222,500. You used a cube 6.5 cm on a side, so a ball filled $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$ of your space.

feedback.correct: 200 to 250 holds the value, about 222.5 thousand, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Multiply the figures step by step, rounding only at the end. Then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: The room is 50 m³, and a ball is $\tfrac{\pi}{6} \times 0.065^3 \approx 0.000144$ m³. So $\tfrac{0.64 \times 50}{0.000144} \approx 222{,}500$ balls, and the same sum in centimetres agrees. The interval 100 to 400 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less on the day.

items.title: Heartbeats in a lifetime
items.question: A heart beats 70 times a minute. How many beats is that in 80 years, in billions? Take a year as 365.25 days. Choose the tightest interval that holds your estimate.

options.why: This sits wholly above the value, 2.945 billion. Rounding the 1,440 minutes in a day up to 1,500 lands here.
This sits wholly below the value, 2.945 billion. Using 60 beats a minute, not 70, lands here.
This holds the value, but 2.8 to 3.0 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.

feedback.correct: 2.8 to 3.0 holds the value, 2.945 billion, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Multiply the figures step by step, rounding only at the end. Then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: A year holds $70 \times 60 \times 24 \times 365.25 = 36{,}817{,}200$ beats. Times 80, that is about 2.945 billion. The interval 2.0 to 4.0 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less on the day.

items.title: Quote updates in a day
items.question: A desk quotes 4 markets. Each quote is updated twice a second for a 6.5-hour day. How many updates is that, in thousands? Choose the tightest interval that holds your estimate.

options.why: This sits wholly below the value, 187,200. With 3,000 seconds an hour you get 156,000: an hour has 3,600.
This sits wholly above the value, 187,200. Rounding 28,800 an hour up to 30,000 gives 195,000: round only at the end.
This holds the value, but 180 to 190 holds it too and is tighter. A wider interval scores less on the day.

feedback.correct: 180 to 190 holds the value, 187,200, and is the tightest that does.
feedback.generic: Multiply the figures step by step, rounding only at the end. Then pick the narrowest interval that holds it.

explain.text: Each hour brings $4 \times 2 \times 3600 = 28{,}800$ updates. Over 6.5 hours that is 187,200. The interval 100 to 300 holds it too, but it is wider, so it scores less on the day.

items.title: Make a market on three dice
items.prose: The game settles at the total of three fair dice, shown one card at a time. Each turn you quote a bid, an ask and a size. A counterparty may then trade at your prices. Later in the game the interviewer may know more than you.
items.question: Finish the eight turns with a P&L of at least £8, and no rule breaks.

schedule.text: Three fair dice will be rolled, one at a time. Their total settles the game. Fair starts at 10.5.
The first die shows 6. Fair is now 13.
The second die shows 4. Fair is now 13.5.
The third die shows 3. The total is 13.

feedback.correct: You moved your quote up with each die and kept it either side of fair.
feedback.generic: After each card, centre your quote on the new fair value and keep your position small.

byKey.low: You kept your opening prices after the first die showed 6, so buyers took your ask below fair.
byKey.limit: You kept quoting 2 a side as your position grew, so a quote passed the limit of 5.
byKey.crossed: You set your bid at or above your ask, so nobody could trade that turn.
byKey.spread: You set a spread outside £1 to £4. Keep the ask £1 to £4 above the bid.

explain.text: The model run bought 2 at £9, then sold 1 at £14.50 after the first die. It held 1 into the total of 13, for a P&L of £9.50. Its later quotes sat either side of fair, so the informed traders had nothing to take.

items.title: Bad news, then informed sellers
items.prose: A share opens at £50 and settles at a hidden value after turn 8. Each turn you quote a bid, an ask and a size. After the news, the traders you meet may know the value.
items.question: Finish the eight turns with a P&L of at least £12, and no rule breaks.

schedule.text: A weak report. Fair is now £48.

feedback.correct: You sold to the noise traders early and kept your bid low once the sellers knew more.
feedback.generic: After a weak report, move your bid well down: an informed seller only hits a bid above the value.

byKey.low: You kept your bid near £48.50 after the weak report, so informed sellers hit it above the value.
byKey.limit: You kept quoting 2 as informed sellers hit your bid, so a quote passed the limit of 4.
byKey.crossed: You set your bid at or above your ask, so nobody could trade that turn.
byKey.spread: You set a spread outside £1 to £5. Keep the ask £1 to £5 above the bid.

explain.text: The model run bought 1 at £48.50 and sold 2 at £51.50 twice, ending short 3. After the report its bid stayed at £46 or lower, so informed sellers had nothing to hit. Short 3 into a value of £46, its P&L was £19.50.

items.title: The interviewer tests your limit
items.prose: The interviewer is your only counterparty and plays to a script. Each turn you quote a bid, an ask and a size. Your position limit is 3 either way. The interviewer may know more than you.
items.question: Finish the six turns with a P&L of at least £6, and no rule breaks.

schedule.text: The interviewer will trade against you. Fair starts at £100, and the position limit is 3.
The interviewer says the level looks higher. Fair is now £102.

feedback.correct: You stepped your bid away before your position reached the limit.
feedback.generic: Watch your position. When the interviewer keeps selling, lower your bid so you stop buying.

byKey.low: You sold to the interviewer too far below the value, or bought too little at £98.
byKey.limit: You kept buying until your position reached the limit of 3. Then even a size of 1 breaks it, so lower your bid before you get there.
byKey.crossed: You set your bid at or above your ask, so nobody could trade that turn.
byKey.spread: You set a spread outside £2 to £6. Keep the ask £2 to £6 above the bid.

explain.text: The model run bought 2 at £98, then bid £96.50 so the interviewer could sell no more. It sold 1 at £102 and 1 at £101 to finish flat, for a P&L of £7. Both sales were under the value of £104: the interviewer knew more.

items.title: Defend your quote
items.prompt:
Say your answer aloud first, then type it.

Fair is £100, your limit is 3 either way, and spreads must be £2 to £6. You bought 2 at £98 on turn 1. The interviewer offers to sell again at £97.50. You quote £96.50 to £100.50 for 1. Explain the quote.
items.model: I am long 2 against a limit of 3, so I have room to buy only 1 more. If the interviewer sold me 2 at £97.50, I would be long 4, over the limit. Even 1 more leaves me at the limit, where any bid breaks it. So my bid of £96.50 sits under their £97.50, and they cannot sell to me. My ask of £100.50 is above fair at £100, so a sale still earns. The quote is skewed down because of my inventory, not a view on the price. A seller who keeps selling may also know more, which is one more reason to stop buying. The width is £4, inside the £2 to £6 allowed. A card, a new price or a fill would change it. So my quote is £96.50 to £100.50 for 1.

rubric.text: States the position, long 2, and the limit of 3
Says the bid sits below the interviewer's £97.50, so no more is bought
Gives the ask against the fair value of £100
Names the skew as inventory management, not a view
Mentions adverse selection: a seller who keeps selling may know more
States what would change the quote: a card, a price or a fill
Reasons aloud, in order, with a clear final quote

items.title: Why trading
items.prompt:
Say your answer aloud first, then type it in at most 200 words.

Why do you want to trade rather than work at a bank or a lab?
items.model:
*An example answer. Your own story is the real answer, so use this for its shape only.*

I want to trade because I like pricing things I cannot know for sure. I also want fast, honest feedback: a trading decision is scored within hours, not years. At university I ran a prediction-market club for 40 students. I set the weekly prices and logged every call. My hit rate rose from 52% to 61% over a term. What I find hard is letting go of a loss. I now write my reason before each trade and review the reason afterwards, not the result. A bank puts the client first, and a lab works on long cycles. A trading firm puts the decision and its feedback at the centre. That is the work I want every day.

rubric.text: Gives a one-sentence answer first
Two reasons tied to the daily work, such as pricing under uncertainty and fast feedback
One piece of your own evidence, with a number or an outcome
Says what you dislike or find hard about trading, and how you handle it
Says why a trading firm rather than another route
Takes about 90 seconds aloud, with no clichés

items.title: A decision without all the facts
items.prompt:
Say your answer aloud first, then type it in at most 200 words.

Tell me about a decision you made with incomplete information, and what you would change.
items.model:
*An example answer. Your own story is the real answer, so use this for its shape only.*

In my second year I led a four-person project with a fixed deadline. Two weeks out, our data supplier stopped replying. I did not know whether the data would arrive in time. I put the chance it would be late at about one in three. Waiting cost nothing if it came, but the whole grade if it did not. Switching to a public data set cost about two days of extra work. So I switched that week. The supplier's data came four days late. We handed in on time with a narrower analysis and scored 68%. I would change one thing. I would set a check-in date with the supplier at the start, so the warning came a week sooner.

rubric.text: Sets out the situation in one or two sentences
Says what you did not know
The decision and its reason, with a rough probability or cost
States the result honestly
Says what you would change, and how you would know sooner
Speaks in the first person, in under two minutes
